citation.title: Randomization-based confidence sets for the local average treatment effect

standing_assumptions: [Units, potential outcomes, compliance: main p. 3 (PDF p. 3), Section 2.1] We consider an experiment with $n$ units, where each unit is randomized to treatment or control. Let $y_i(d, z)$ denote the potential outcome of unit $i$ under the potential compliance decision $d \in \{0, 1\}$ and the treatment assignment $z \in \{0, 1\}$. Let $d_i(z)$ denote the compliance decision of the $i$th unit when under treatment status $z$. We write $d_i(1) = 0$ if the $i$th unit is assigned to treatment, but does not receive treatment, and write $d_i(1) = 1$ if it does. The compliance decision $d_i(0)$ under assignment to control is defined analogously. [...] Let $[n] = \{1, \ldots, n\}$. Assumption 1 (Exclusion restriction). For all $i \in [n]$, $y_i(d, z)$ is independent of $z$. This assumption implies that treatment assignment affects outcomes only through treatment receipt, and hence $y_i(d, 1) = y_i(d, 0)$ for all $i \in [n]$. Given this assumption, we write $y_i(d)$ from now on to denote the potential outcome under treatment status $d$. [main p. 4 (PDF p. 4)] Assumption 2 (Monotonicity). For all $i \in [n]$, we have $d_i(1) \ge d_i(0)$. Let $\mathcal{C}$ denote the set of compliers, $\mathcal{C} = \{i \in [n] : d_i(0) = 0,\ d_i(1) = 1\}$. (1) Our inferential target is the LATE in the experimental sample, defined by $\bar\beta = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}|}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{C}}\{y_i(1) - y_i(0)\}$. (2) We assume throughout the paper that there is at least one complier ($|\mathcal{C}| \ge 1$) so that the quantity is well-defined. [Design and data: main p. 4, Section 2.2] We assume that the experiments under consideration are completely randomized: among $n$ units, researchers assign $n_1$ units to treatment, chosen uniformly at random. [...] For each unit $i$, we let $Z_i$ be a random variable such that $Z_i = 1$ if unit $i$ is assigned to treatment and $Z_i = 0$ otherwise. By definition, $\mathrm{pr}(Z_i = 1) = n_1/n$, and we introduce the shorthand $\pi = n_1/n$. For each unit $i$, researchers observe compliance decisions $D_i = d_i(Z_i)$ and outcomes $Y_i = y_i(D_i)$. Each unit $i$ may additionally be associated with some covariate information [...]; if so, this information is collected in a column vector $x_i \in \mathbb{R}^k$. Throughout the paper we assume that $k$ does not change with the sample size $n$. [...] We adopt the finite-population (design-based) framework, treating the potential outcomes and compliance decisions as fixed parameters [...]. The sole source of randomness in our model is the vector of random treatment assignments, and statistical uncertainties are evaluated exclusively with respect to this randomness. [Studentized statistic: main pp. 4-5, Section 3.1] For all $\beta \in \mathbb{R}$, we define the statistic $\hat\tau(\beta) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \beta D_i)(Z_i - \pi)$. [...] A short calculation shows that $\hat\tau(\beta) = \pi(1-\pi)\left\{\frac{1}{n_1}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i(Y_i - \beta D_i) - \frac{1}{n_0}\sum_{i=1}^n (1 - Z_i)(Y_i - \beta D_i)\right\}$, where $n_0 = n - n_1$ [...]. We further define $\hat v_i(1, \beta) = Y_i - \beta D_i - \frac{1}{n_1}\sum_{j=1}^n Z_j(Y_j - \beta D_j)$, $\hat v_i(0, \beta) = Y_i - \beta D_i - \frac{1}{n_0}\sum_{j=1}^n (1 - Z_j)(Y_j - \beta D_j)$. (3) Using this notation, we define the variance estimator $\hat\sigma^2(\beta) = \frac{\pi^2(1-\pi)^2}{n_1^2}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i\hat v_i^2(1, \beta) + \frac{\pi^2(1-\pi)^2}{n_0^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (1 - Z_i)\hat v_i^2(0, \beta)$ and the studentized statistic $\Delta(\beta) = \frac{\hat\tau(\beta)}{\hat\sigma(\beta)}$. (4) We will use the absolute value $|\Delta(\beta)|$ as our test statistic and construct confidence sets by test inversion. We refer to the test statistic $\Delta(\beta)$ in (4) as the AR statistic. [Randomization distribution and confidence set: main pp. 5-6, Section 3.2] The assignment vector $Z = (Z_1, \ldots, Z_n)$ is a random vector in $\{0, 1\}^n$. Let $Z^*$ be a random vector with the same distribution as $Z$ and which is independent of $Z$. We use $\mathbb{P}^*$ to denote the conditional (on $Z$) probability measure induced by $Z^*$. We define $\hat\tau^* : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ by $\hat\tau^*(\beta) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \beta D_i)(Z_i^* - \pi)$, where we recall that by definition $Y_i$ and $D_i$ depend only on $Z_i$ and not on $Z_i^*$. We also define the variance estimator $\hat\sigma^{*2}(\beta) = \frac{\pi^2(1-\pi)^2}{n_1^2}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i^*\left\{Y_i - \beta D_i - \frac{1}{n_1}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i^*(Y_i - \beta D_i)\right\}^2 + \frac{\pi^2(1-\pi)^2}{n_0^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (1 - Z_i^*)\left\{Y_i - \beta D_i - \frac{1}{n_0}\sum_{i=1}^n (1 - Z_i^*)(Y_i - \beta D_i)\right\}^2$ [the inner sums are the reassigned-arm means; the paper reuses the index $i$] and the studentized statistic $\Delta^*(\beta) = \frac{\hat\tau^*(\beta)}{\hat\sigma^*(\beta)}$. (5) The distribution of $|\Delta^*(\beta)|$ under $\mathbb{P}^*$ is discrete and supported on $[0, \infty]$. For every $\alpha \in (0, 1)$, there exists a smallest (possibly infinite) value $\eta^*_{1-\alpha}(\beta, Z)$ such that $\mathbb{P}^*\{|\Delta^*(\beta)| \le \eta^*_{1-\alpha}(\beta, Z)\} \ge 1 - \alpha$. (6) Our confidence set is defined as $I^*_{1-\alpha}(Z) = \{\beta \in \mathbb{R} : |\Delta(\beta)| \le \eta^*_{1-\alpha}(\beta, Z)\}$. (7) [Assumptions 3 and 4, parameter space $\Theta_n$: main pp. 6-8] Assumption 3 (Parameter space). Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and constants $\delta < 1$ and $A > 0$ be given. Set $w_i(1) = y_i\{d_i(1)\} - \bar\beta d_i(1)$, $w_i(0) = y_i\{d_i(0)\} - \bar\beta d_i(0)$. The following conditions on the potential outcomes and compliance decisions hold. (i) For the given $\delta$, $\sigma_{w(1),w(0),\mathcal{C}} \ge -\delta\,\sigma_{w(1),\mathcal{C}}\,\sigma_{w(0),\mathcal{C}}$. Here, $\sigma_{w(1),w(0),\mathcal{C}}$ is the complier-group covariance of adjusted potential outcomes, $\sigma_{w(1),w(0),\mathcal{C}} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}| - 1}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{C}}\{w_i(1) - \mu_{w(1),\mathcal{C}}\}\{w_i(0) - \mu_{w(0),\mathcal{C}}\}$, where $\mu_{w(a),\mathcal{C}} = |\mathcal{C}|^{-1}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{C}} w_i(a)$ for $a \in \{0, 1\}$, and $\sigma^2_{w(1),\mathcal{C}}$ and $\sigma^2_{w(0),\mathcal{C}}$ are the complier-group potential outcome variances, $\sigma^2_{w(a),\mathcal{C}} = \frac{1}{|\mathcal{C}| - 1}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{C}}\{w_i(a) - \mu_{w(a),\mathcal{C}}\}^2$ for $a \in \{0, 1\}$. If $|\mathcal{C}| = 1$, all variances and covariances are defined to be zero. (ii) For each $a \in \{0, 1\}$ and the given $A$, $\left\{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n |w_i(a) - \mu_{w(a)}|^4\right\}^{1/4} \le A\sigma_{w(a)}$, where $\mu_{w(a)} = n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n w_i(a)$ and $\sigma^2_{w(a)} = (n-1)^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n \{w_i(a) - \mu_{w(a)}\}^2$. [...] Assumption 4 (Completely randomized experiment). Given $n \in \mathbb{N}$ and a constant $0 < r \le 1/2$, we have $n_1 \in [rn, (1-r)n]$. We denote the parameter space of potential outcomes, compliance decisions and experimental designs satisfying Assumptions 1-4 with $n$ units and constants $\delta$, $r$ and $A$ by $\Theta_n(\delta, r, A) = \left\{\left(\{(y_i(1), y_i(0), d_i(1), d_i(0))\}_{i=1}^n, \Pi_n\right)\right\}$, where $\{(y_i(1), y_i(0), d_i(1), d_i(0))\}_{i=1}^n$ satisfies Assumption 3 with constants $\delta$ and $A$, and $\Pi_n$ is a distribution of random assignment variables $\{Z_i\}_{i=1}^n$ implementing complete randomization that satisfies Assumption 4 with constant $r$. Each combination of potential outcomes, compliance decisions and an experimental design completely determines the distribution of our test statistic. [...] For each parameter $\theta$ in the parameter space, we denote its LATE by $\bar\beta(\theta)$. [Regression adjustment: main pp. 8-10, Sections 4.1-4.3] [...] each unit $i$ comes equipped with a column vector $x_i \in \mathbb{R}^k$ of covariates for some $k \in \mathbb{N}$. We suppose that each $x_i$ is demeaned, meaning that $\sum_{i=1}^n x_i = 0_k$, where $0_k$ denotes the zero vector in $\mathbb{R}^k$. [...] We denote the $s$th element of $x_i$ by $x_{si}$. Given a $\beta \in \mathbb{R}$ and a treatment assignment vector $Z$, consider the linear regression $Y_i - \beta D_i \sim (1 - Z_i)\varphi_0 + Z_i\varphi_1 + (1 - Z_i)x_i'\gamma_0 + Z_i x_i'\gamma_1$. (8) This is an interacted linear regression that regresses $Y_i - \beta D_i$ on $((1 - Z_i), Z_i, (1 - Z_i)x_i, Z_i x_i)$ without an intercept. For each $\beta$, denote the ordinary least squares (OLS) estimators resulting from (8) by $\hat\varphi(0, \beta)$, $\hat\varphi(1, \beta)$, $\hat\gamma(0, \beta)$ and $\hat\gamma(1, \beta)$, corresponding to the order in which the associated coefficients appear in (8). We define the randomization statistics $\hat\varphi^*(0, \beta)$, $\hat\varphi^*(1, \beta)$, $\hat\gamma^*(0, \beta)$ and $\hat\gamma^*(1, \beta)$ similarly by using $Z^*$ instead of $Z$. [main p. 9] We define the covariate-adjusted difference-in-means statistic as $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta) = \frac{1}{n_1}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i\{Y_i - \beta D_i - x_i'\hat\gamma(1, \beta)\} - \frac{1}{n_0}\sum_{i=1}^n (1 - Z_i)\{Y_i - \beta D_i - x_i'\hat\gamma(0, \beta)\}$, (9) and we define the covariate-adjusted randomization estimator $\hat\tau^*_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)$ analogously, again replacing $Z_i$ by $Z_i^*$ and replacing $\hat\gamma(0, \beta)$ and $\hat\gamma(1, \beta)$ by their randomization analogues. [...] The residual estimators associated with (8) and their randomization-based counterparts are $\hat\varepsilon_i(\beta) = Y_i - \beta D_i - \hat\varphi(Z_i, \beta) - x_i'\hat\gamma(Z_i, \beta)$, $\hat\varepsilon_i^*(\beta) = Y_i - \beta D_i - \hat\varphi^*(Z_i^*, \beta) - x_i'\hat\gamma^*(Z_i^*, \beta)$. We use these to define the variance estimators $\hat\sigma^2_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta) = \frac{1}{n_1^2}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i\hat\varepsilon_i(\beta)^2 + \frac{1}{n_0^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (1 - Z_i)\hat\varepsilon_i(\beta)^2$, $\hat\sigma^{2*}_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta) = \frac{1}{n_1^2}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i^*\hat\varepsilon_i^*(\beta)^2 + \frac{1}{n_0^2}\sum_{i=1}^n (1 - Z_i^*)\hat\varepsilon_i^*(\beta)^2$. The adjusted studentized difference-in-means statistics are then $\Delta_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta) = \frac{\hat\tau_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)}{\hat\sigma_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)}$, $\Delta^*_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta) = \frac{\hat\tau^*_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)}{\hat\sigma^*_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)}$. (10) [...] Given $\alpha \in (0, 1)$, there exists a smallest (possibly infinite) value $\eta^{\mathrm{adj},*}_{1-\alpha}(\beta, Z)$ such that $\mathbb{P}^*\{|\Delta^*_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)| \le \eta^{\mathrm{adj},*}_{1-\alpha}(\beta, Z)\} \ge 1 - \alpha$. [main p. 10] Our proposed confidence set is $I^{\mathrm{adj},*}_{1-\alpha}(Z) = \{\beta \in \mathbb{R} : |\Delta_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)| \le \eta^{\mathrm{adj},*}_{1-\alpha}(\beta, Z)\}$. (11) [Assumption 5 and parameter space $\Xi_n$: main pp. 10-11] Assumption 5. Let $k, n \in \mathbb{N}$ and constants $\delta < 1$ and $\tilde\varepsilon, A, B > 0$ be given. For each $a \in \{0, 1\}$, define $\varepsilon_i(a, \bar\beta) = y_i\{d_i(a)\} - \bar\beta d_i(a) - \varphi(a, \bar\beta) - x_i'\gamma(a, \bar\beta)$. The following conditions on the potential outcomes, compliance decisions and covariates hold. (i) For the given $\delta$, $\sigma_{\varepsilon(1,\bar\beta),\varepsilon(0,\bar\beta)} \ge -\delta\sigma_{\varepsilon(1,\bar\beta)}\sigma_{\varepsilon(0,\bar\beta)}$. (ii) For each $a \in \{0, 1\}$ and the given $B$, $\left\{\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \varepsilon_i^4(a, \bar\beta)\right\}^{1/4} \le B\sigma_{\varepsilon(a,\bar\beta)}$. (iii) We have that $\sum_{i=1}^n x_i = 0_k$. (iv) For all $s \in [k]$ and the given $A$, we have that $n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n x_{si}^4 \le A$. (v) Let $\lambda_{\min}$ denote the smallest eigenvalue of $n^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n x_i x_i'$. Then for the given $\tilde\varepsilon$, $\lambda_{\min} \ge \tilde\varepsilon$. We denote the parameter space of potential outcomes, compliance decisions, covariates and experimental designs satisfying Assumptions 1, 2, 4 and 5 with $n$ units, covariates of dimension $k$, and constants $\delta$, $\tilde\varepsilon$, $A$, $B$ and $r$ by $\Xi_n(k, \delta, \tilde\varepsilon, A, B, r) = \left\{\left(\{(y_i(1), y_i(0), d_i(1), d_i(0), x_i)\}_{i=1}^n, \Pi_n\right)\right\}$. Here, $\{(y_i(1), y_i(0), d_i(1), d_i(0), x_i)\}_{i=1}^n$ satisfies Assumption 5 with constants $\delta$, $\tilde\varepsilon$, $A$ and $B$, and $\Pi_n$ is a distribution of random assignment variables $\{Z_i\}_{i=1}^n$ implementing complete randomization that satisfies Assumption 4 with constant $r$. [The population variances and covariance in Assumption 5 are those of Supplement A.1 below, with divisor $n - 1$; $\varphi(a, \beta)$, $\gamma(a, \beta)$ are defined in Supplement D.2 below.] [Supplement A, notation: Supplement p. 21 (Supplement PDF p. 1)] We let $\mathbb{N}$ denote the positive integers [...]. We use the notation $\lesssim$ to denote inequalities that hold up to a constant independent of $n$. [...] We also define a set $\mathcal{A}$ of always-takers and a set $\mathcal{N}$ of never-takers by $\mathcal{A} = \{i \in [n] : d_i(0) = 1, d_i(1) = 1\}$, $\mathcal{N} = \{i \in [n] : d_i(0) = 0, d_i(1) = 0\}$. Let $\mathcal{T}(1), \mathcal{T}(0) \subset [n]$ denote the sets of subjects in the treatment and control groups defined by $Z$, respectively, so that $\mathcal{T}(1) = \{i \in [n] : Z_i = 1\}$, $\mathcal{T}(0) = \{i \in [n] : Z_i = 0\}$. Given a vector $v$, we use $\|v\|_2$ to denote the standard $l_2$ vector norm. [...] A.1. For any vector $q = (q_i)_{i=1}^n \in \mathbb{R}^n$, we define the population mean and variance by $\mu_q = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n q_i$, $\sigma_q^2 = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (q_i - \mu_q)^2$. We also define within-group variances for each group $G \in \{\mathcal{A}, \mathcal{C}, \mathcal{N}\}$ by $\sigma^2_{q,G} = \frac{1}{|G| - 1}\sum_{i \in G}(q_i - \mu_{q,G})^2$, where $\mu_{q,G} = \frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{i \in G} q_i$ if $|G| \ge 2$ and zero otherwise. Given an additional vector $\tilde q = (\tilde q_i)_{i=1}^n \in \mathbb{R}^n$, we define the population covariance by $\sigma_{q\tilde q} = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (q_i - \mu_q)(\tilde q_i - \mu_{\tilde q})$, and the within-group covariances by $\sigma_{q\tilde q,G} = \frac{1}{|G| - 1}\sum_{i \in G}(q_i - \mu_{q,G})(\tilde q_i - \mu_{\tilde q,G})$, if $|G| \ge 2$ and zero otherwise. A.2. Let $\mathcal{Z}$ be a mean zero, variance one normal random variable. [...] For an $\alpha \in (0, 1)$, define $z_{1-\alpha} \in \mathbb{R}$ as the value such that $\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{Z} > z_{1-\alpha}) = \alpha$. [Supplement B.1 and B.3: Supplement p. 22 (PDF p. 2)] Lemma 2. For all $\beta \in \mathbb{R}$, the variance of $\hat\tau(\beta)$ is $\operatorname{var}(\hat\tau(\beta)) = \frac{S_1^2(\beta)}{n_1} + \frac{S_0^2(\beta)}{n_0} - \frac{S_{10}^2(\beta)}{n}$, (B.1) where $S_1^2(\beta) = \frac{\pi^2(1-\pi)^2}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n v_i(1, \beta)^2$, $S_0^2(\beta) = \frac{\pi^2(1-\pi)^2}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n v_i(0, \beta)^2$, $S_{10}^2(\beta) = \frac{\pi^2(1-\pi)^2}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (v_i(1, \beta) - v_i(0, \beta))^2$, (B.2) $v_i(1, \beta) = y_i(d_i(1)) - \beta d_i(1) - \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i(d_i(1)) - \beta d_i(1))$, (B.3) $v_i(0, \beta) = y_i(d_i(0)) - \beta d_i(0) - \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i(d_i(0)) - \beta d_i(0))$. (B.4) [...] Lemma 3. We have $E[\hat\tau(\beta)] = 0$ when $\beta = |\mathcal{C}|^{-1}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{C}}(y_i(1) - y_i(0))$. [Supplement C, conventions: Supplement p. 23 (PDF p. 3)] Throughout this section, we let $\delta, r, A$ be the constants fixed in the statement of Theorem 1, and set $\Theta_n = \Theta_n(\delta, r, A)$. The notation $\Theta_n$ encodes Assumptions 1-4. We typically denote elements of $\Theta_n$ by $\theta_n$. For each model $\theta_n$, we denote its local average treatment effect by $\bar\beta(\theta_n)$ [...]. In various lemmas below, we will consider subsequences $(\theta_{n_k})_{k=1}^\infty$ of a given sequence $(\theta_n)_{n=1}^\infty$ of models. We let $n_{1k}$ denote the number of elements in the treatment group of $\theta_{n_k}$, and $n_{0k}$ the number of elements in the control group of $\theta_{n_k}$, so that $n_{0k} + n_{1k} = n_k$. [...] For the remainder of the proofs, we will implicitly assume that the variances $\sigma^2_{w(a)}$, for $a \in \{0, 1\}$ as defined in Assumption 3, are both strictly positive. This entails no loss of generality provided we adopt the convention that $0/0 = 0$. If both variances are zero, then the complier treatment effect is constant and additive, so the exact coverage result of the randomization-based CI in Imbens & Rosenbaum (2005) applies. [...] Similar comments apply to the proofs in Section D. [...] In results on sequences $(\theta_n)_{n=1}^\infty$, we will generally omit the $n$-dependence on $w_i(1)$, $w_i(0)$, and other model-dependent quantities for brevity. [Supplement C.3: Supplement pp. 27-28 (PDF pp. 7-8)] We write $E^*$ and $\operatorname{var}^*$ for expectation and variance under the probability measure $\mathbb{P}^*$. By Lemma 3, for any $\beta$ we have $E^*[\hat\tau^*(\beta)] = 0$, and by Lemma 2, $\operatorname{var}^*(\hat\tau^*(\beta)) = \frac{S_1^{*2}(\beta)}{n_1} + \frac{S_0^{*2}(\beta)}{n_0}$, (C.25) where $S_1^{*2}(\beta) = S_0^{*2}(\beta) = \frac{\pi^2(1-\pi)^2}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n \left(Y_i - \beta D_i - \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \beta D_i)\right)^2$. (C.26) [...] We recall that $\mu_Y = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n Y_i$, $\mu_D = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n D_i$ and define $\hat\mu_{y(d(a))} = \frac{1}{n_a}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{T}(a)} y_i(d_i(a))$, $\hat\mu_{d(a)} = \frac{1}{n_a}\sum_{i \in \mathcal{T}(a)} d_i(a)$, for each $a \in \{0, 1\}$. [Supplement D, least-squares parameters and infeasible estimator: Supplement pp. 31-32 (PDF pp. 11-12)] We let $k, \delta, \tilde\varepsilon, A, B, r$ be the constants fixed in the statement of Theorem 2, and set $\Xi_n = \Xi_n(k, \delta, \tilde\varepsilon, A, B, r)$. D.2. Suppose a $\beta \in \mathbb{R}$ is given. Then we define, for each $a \in \{0, 1\}$, outcomes $w_i(a, \beta)$ by $w_i(a, \beta) = y_i(d_i(a)) - \beta d_i(a)$. (D.1) We define the least-squares regression parameters $\varphi(a, \beta) : \{0, 1\} \times \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, $\gamma(a, \beta) : \{0, 1\} \times \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}^k$, by $(\varphi(a, \beta), \gamma(a, \beta)) = \arg\min_{(s,t) \in \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R}^k}\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n (w_i(a, \beta) - s - x_i't)^2$, (D.2) where we interpret $t$ as a column vector. We define the residuals for (D.2) by $\varepsilon_i(a, \beta) = w_i(a, \beta) - \varphi(a, \beta) - x_i'\gamma(a, \beta)$. The parameters $\varphi^*(a, \beta)$ and $\gamma^*(a, \beta)$ are defined similarly, by replacing $w_i(a, \beta)$ with $Y_i - \beta D_i$ in (D.2), and we define the associated residuals $\varepsilon_i^*(\beta)$ by $\varepsilon_i^*(\beta) = Y_i - \beta D_i - \varphi^*(a, \beta) - x_i'\gamma^*(a, \beta)$. (D.3) These definitions imply that $\varphi^*(0, \beta) = \varphi^*(1, \beta)$ and $\gamma^*(0, \beta) = \gamma^*(1, \beta)$. D.3. To analyze the asymptotic behavior of $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)$, we define the infeasible estimator $\tilde\tau_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta) = \frac{1}{n_1}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i(Y_i - \beta D_i - x_i'\gamma(1, \beta)) - \frac{1}{n_0}\sum_{i=1}^n (1 - Z_i)(Y_i - \beta D_i - x_i'\gamma(0, \beta))$. (D.4) The infeasible estimator $\tilde\tau^*_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)$ is defined similarly, replacing $Z_i$ by $Z_i^*$, and $\gamma(1, \beta)$ and $\gamma(0, \beta)$ by $\gamma^*(1, \beta)$ and $\gamma^*(0, \beta)$, respectively. A straightforward adaptation of Lemma 2 shows that $\operatorname{var}(\tilde\tau_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)) = \frac{\mathcal{S}_1^2(\beta)}{n_1} + \frac{\mathcal{S}_0^2(\beta)}{n_0} - \frac{\mathcal{S}_{10}^2(\beta)}{n}$, (D.5) where $\mathcal{S}_1^2(\beta) = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n \varepsilon_i^2(1, \beta)$, $\mathcal{S}_0^2(\beta) = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n \varepsilon_i^2(0, \beta)$, $\mathcal{S}_{10}^2(\beta) = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (\varepsilon_i(1, \beta) - \varepsilon_i(0, \beta))^2$. Similarly, $\operatorname{var}^*(\tilde\tau^*_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)) = \frac{\mathcal{S}_{1,*}^2(\beta)}{n_1} + \frac{\mathcal{S}_{0,*}^2(\beta)}{n_0}$, $\mathcal{S}_{1,*}^2(\beta) = \mathcal{S}_{0,*}^2(\beta) = \frac{1}{n-1}\sum_{i=1}^n \varepsilon_i^*(\beta)^2$. (D.6) [Supplement E.1: Supplement p. 32 (PDF p. 12)] Denote $x_i^\circ = [0, x_i']' \in \mathbb{R}^{k+1}$ and $\tilde x_i = [1, x_i']' \in \mathbb{R}^{k+1}$. For $a \in \{0, 1\}$, define $\psi(a, \beta) = \begin{bmatrix}\varphi(a, \beta) \\ \gamma(a, \beta)\end{bmatrix}$, $\hat\psi(a, \beta) = \begin{bmatrix}\hat\varphi(a, \beta) \\ \hat\gamma(a, \beta)\end{bmatrix}$. (E.1) We denote their randomization counterparts as $\psi^*(a, \beta)$ and $\hat\psi^*(a, \beta)$. Lemma 14. The following claims hold. 1. We have $\hat\psi(1, \beta) - \psi(1, \beta) = \left(\frac{1}{n_1}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i\tilde x_i\tilde x_i'\right)^{-1}\frac{1}{n_1}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i\tilde x_i\varepsilon_i(1, \beta)$ (E.2) and $\hat\psi(0, \beta) - \psi(0, \beta) = \left(\frac{1}{n_0}\sum_{i=1}^n (1 - Z_i)\tilde x_i\tilde x_i'\right)^{-1}\frac{1}{n_0}\sum_{i=1}^n (1 - Z_i)\tilde x_i\varepsilon_i(0, \beta)$, (E.3) provided that the matrices $\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i\tilde x_i\tilde x_i'$ and $\sum_{i=1}^n (1 - Z_i)\tilde x_i\tilde x_i'$ are invertible. 2. For each $a \in \{0, 1\}$, $\sum_{i=1}^n \tilde x_i\varepsilon_i(a, \beta) = 0_{k+1}$. canonical_claim.name_in_paper: Remark 4: the regression-adjusted Wald estimator (12) zeroes the adjusted statistic and equals the coefficient on $D_i$ in the interacted instrumental variable regression
canonical_claim.location: Main p. 10 (PDF p. 10), Remark 4 and equation (12); algebra in Supplement Section I, pp. 45-47 (Supplement PDF pp. 25-27)
canonical_claim.statement: [As printed, main p. 10] Remark 4. The set $I^{\mathrm{adj},*}_{1-\alpha}(Z)$ may not necessarily form a single interval, but is generally a finite union of intervals when it is nonempty. The regression-adjusted Wald estimator, defined as $\hat\beta^{\mathrm{adj}}_{\mathrm{Wald}} = \frac{n_1^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i(Y_i - x_i'\hat\gamma_{y,1}) - n_0^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (1 - Z_i)(Y_i - x_i'\hat\gamma_{y,0})}{n_1^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i(D_i - x_i'\hat\gamma_{d,1}) - n_0^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (1 - Z_i)(D_i - x_i'\hat\gamma_{d,0})}$, (12) always lies within this set (because $\Delta_{\mathrm{adj}}(\hat\beta^{\mathrm{adj}}_{\mathrm{Wald}}) = 0$) provided that it is well-defined (i.e., the denominator is not zero). The coefficients $\hat\gamma_{y,1}$ and $\hat\gamma_{y,0}$ are the OLS estimators obtained from the interacted regression $Y_i \sim \alpha_{y,0} + \alpha_{y,1}Z_i + Z_i x_i'\gamma_{y,1} + (1 - Z_i)x_i'\gamma_{y,0}$, while $\hat\gamma_{d,1}$ and $\hat\gamma_{d,0}$ are the OLS estimators from the regression $D_i \sim \alpha_{d,0} + \alpha_{d,1}Z_i + Z_i x_i'\gamma_{d,1} + (1 - Z_i)x_i'\gamma_{d,0}$. The estimator $\hat\beta^{\mathrm{adj}}_{\mathrm{Wald}}$ is also algebraically equivalent to the coefficient of $D_i$ in the instrumental variable regression $Y_i \sim \alpha + \alpha_1 D_i + Z_i x_i'\gamma_1 + (1 - Z_i)x_i'\gamma_0$, where the instruments are $1$, $Z_i$, $Z_i x_i$ and $(1 - Z_i)x_i$ when both estimators are well-defined (i.e., the denominator is not zero and the design matrix is invertible). These algebraic relationships are documented in the Supplementary Material. [Formal content] For an assignment $Z$ for which each arm's design matrix $(1, x_i')$ has full column rank: (a) for every $\beta \in \mathbb{R}$, $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta) = N_y - \beta N_d$, where $N_y$ and $N_d$ are the numerator and the denominator of (12); (b) if $N_d \ne 0$, then $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{adj}}(\hat\beta^{\mathrm{adj}}_{\mathrm{Wald}}) = 0$, hence $\Delta_{\mathrm{adj}}(\hat\beta^{\mathrm{adj}}_{\mathrm{Wald}}) = 0$ and $\hat\beta^{\mathrm{adj}}_{\mathrm{Wald}} \in I^{\mathrm{adj},*}_{1-\alpha}(Z)$ for every $\alpha \in (0, 1)$; (c) with $\tilde X_i = (D_i, 1, Z_i x_i', (1 - Z_i)x_i')'$ and $\tilde W_i = (Z_i, 1, Z_i x_i', (1 - Z_i)x_i')'$, if $\sum_{i=1}^n \tilde W_i\tilde X_i'$ and $\sum_{i=1}^n \tilde W_i\tilde W_i'$ are invertible, the first component $\hat\alpha_{1,\mathrm{IV}}$ of the just-identified instrumental variable estimator $\left(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \tilde W_i\tilde X_i'\right)^{-1}\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \tilde W_i Y_i$ (I.3) satisfies $\hat\alpha_{d,1}\hat\alpha_{1,\mathrm{IV}} = \hat\alpha_{y,1}$, where $\hat\alpha_{y,1} = N_y$ and $\hat\alpha_{d,1} = N_d$ are the OLS coefficients on $Z_i$ in the two interacted regressions above, so that $\hat\alpha_{1,\mathrm{IV}} = \hat\beta^{\mathrm{adj}}_{\mathrm{Wald}}$ provided $\hat\alpha_{d,1} \ne 0$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Standing assumptions: demeaned covariates $x_i \in \mathbb{R}^k$, regression (8), $\hat\gamma(a, \beta)$, $\hat\tau_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)$ (9), $\hat\sigma_{\mathrm{adj}}$, $\Delta_{\mathrm{adj}}(\beta)$ (10), $I^{\mathrm{adj},*}_{1-\alpha}(Z)$ (11) (main pp. 8-10); the convention $0/0 = 0$ (Supplement p. 23). [Supplement Section I, pp. 46-47 (PDF pp. 26-27), as printed] We now show that the estimator $\hat\beta^{\mathrm{adj}}_{\mathrm{Wald}}$ is algebraically equivalent to the coefficient for $D_i$ in the instrumental variable (IV) regression $Y_i \sim \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 D_i + \gamma_1 Z_i x_i + \gamma_0(1 - Z_i)x_i$, with the instruments $1$, $Z_i$, $Z_i x_i$, and $(1 - Z_i)x_i$, when both estimators are well-defined (i.e., the denominator is not zero and the design matrix is invertible). [...] $\tilde X_i = (D_i, 1, Z_i x_i', (1 - Z_i)x_i')'$ and $\tilde W_i = (Z_i, 1, Z_i x_i', (1 - Z_i)x_i')'$. We assume that $\sum_{i=1}^n \tilde W_i\tilde X_i'$ and $\sum_{i=1}^n \tilde W_i\tilde W_i'$ are invertible so that the operations below are well-defined. The just-identified IV estimator can be represented as: $\begin{bmatrix}\hat\alpha_{1,\mathrm{IV}} \\ \hat\alpha_{0,\mathrm{IV}} \\ \hat\gamma_{1,\mathrm{IV}} \\ \hat\gamma_{0,\mathrm{IV}}\end{bmatrix} = \left(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \tilde W_i\tilde X_i'\right)^{-1}\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \tilde W_i Y_i$. (I.3) We can further represent the estimator as $\left(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \tilde W_i\tilde X_i'\right)^{-1}\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \tilde W_i\tilde W_i'\left(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \tilde W_i\tilde W_i'\right)^{-1}\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \tilde W_i Y_i$. The first-stage regression can be written as $\left(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \tilde W_i\tilde W_i'\right)^{-1}\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \tilde W_i\tilde X_i' = \left(\begin{array}{c|c}\hat\alpha_{d,1} & 0 \ldots 0 \\ \hline \begin{array}{c}\hat\alpha_{d,0} \\ \hat\gamma_{d,1} \\ \hat\gamma_{d,0}\end{array} & I_{2k+1}\end{array}\right)$, (I.4) where $I_{2k+1}$ is the $(2k+1) \times (2k+1)$ identity matrix, and $\hat\alpha_{d,1}$, $\hat\alpha_{d,0}$, $\hat\gamma_{d,1}$, and $\hat\gamma_{d,0}$ are the OLS estimators from the corresponding regression: $D_i \sim \alpha_{d,1}Z_i + \alpha_{d,0} + Z_i x_i'\gamma_{d,1} + (1 - Z_i)x_i'\gamma_{d,0}$. The reduced-form regression estimator can be written as $\left(\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \tilde W_i\tilde W_i'\right)^{-1}\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n \tilde W_i Y_i = \begin{bmatrix}\hat\alpha_{y,1} \\ \hat\alpha_{y,0} \\ \hat\gamma_{y,1} \\ \hat\gamma_{y,0}\end{bmatrix}$, where $\hat\alpha_{y,1}$, $\hat\alpha_{y,0}$, $\hat\gamma_{y,1}$, and $\hat\gamma_{y,0}$ are the OLS estimators from the corresponding regression: $Y_i \sim \alpha_{y,1}Z_i + \alpha_{y,0} + Z_i x_i'\gamma_{y,1} + (1 - Z_i)x_i'\gamma_{y,0}$. Equation (I.3) implies that the IV estimator satisfies the identity [(I.4) matrix] $\times \begin{bmatrix}\hat\alpha_{1,\mathrm{IV}} \\ \hat\alpha_{0,\mathrm{IV}} \\ \hat\gamma_{1,\mathrm{IV}} \\ \hat\gamma_{0,\mathrm{IV}}\end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix}\hat\alpha_{y,1} \\ \hat\alpha_{y,0} \\ \hat\gamma_{y,1} \\ \hat\gamma_{y,0}\end{bmatrix}$. The first row of the matrix identity implies $\hat\alpha_{d,1}\hat\alpha_{1,\mathrm{IV}} = \hat\alpha_{y,1}$. By the OLS representation in Lin (2013), we have: $\hat\alpha_{y,1} = \frac{1}{n_1}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i\left(Y_i - x_i'\hat\gamma_{y,1}\right) - \frac{1}{n_0}\sum_{i=1}^n (1 - Z_i)\left(Y_i - x_i'\hat\gamma_{y,0}\right)$ and $\hat\alpha_{d,1} = \frac{1}{n_1}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i\left(D_i - x_i'\hat\gamma_{d,1}\right) - \frac{1}{n_0}\sum_{i=1}^n (1 - Z_i)\left(D_i - x_i'\hat\gamma_{d,0}\right)$. Hence, provided that $\hat\alpha_{d,1}$ is nonzero, $\hat\alpha_{1,\mathrm{IV}} = \frac{n_1^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i\left(Y_i - x_i'\hat\gamma_{y,1}\right) - n_0^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (1 - Z_i)\left(Y_i - x_i'\hat\gamma_{y,0}\right)}{n_1^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n Z_i\left(D_i - x_i'\hat\gamma_{d,1}\right) - n_0^{-1}\sum_{i=1}^n (1 - Z_i)\left(D_i - x_i'\hat\gamma_{d,0}\right)} = \hat\beta^{\mathrm{adj}}_{\mathrm{Wald}}$, as desired. [The first step of Section I, (I.1)-(I.2), is given in corrected form in target P002-T24.]
canonical_claim.note: An exact finite-sample algebraic statement; the formal content (a)-(c) was written here from Remark 4 and Supplement Section I. Both readers re-derived the block identity (I.3)-(I.4) and checked it numerically. (a) uses (I.1)-(I.2), whose printed symbols $\hat\tau_{y,z}$, $\hat\tau_{d,z}$ stand for $\hat\gamma_{y,z}$, $\hat\gamma_{d,z}$ (P002-T24). canonical_claim.statement: [As printed, main p. 14] Lemma 1. Consider an open interval $(\beta_1, \beta_2)$, where it is possible that $\beta_1 = -\infty$ or $\beta_2 = \infty$. Under Assumption 6, and supposing that there is no intersection between the AR functions $\{\Delta_m^{*2}(\beta)\}_{m=1}^M$ in $(\beta_1, \beta_2)$, the following hold: (i) the index set $\mathcal{I}(\beta)$ remains the same on $(\beta_1, \beta_2)$; (ii) $\mathcal{I}(\beta) \subset \mathcal{I}(\beta_1) \cap \mathcal{I}(\beta_2)$ for all $\beta \in (\beta_1, \beta_2)$ if both $\beta_1 \in \mathbb{R}$ and $\beta_2 \in \mathbb{R}$; (iii) $\mathcal{I}(\beta) \subset \mathcal{I}(\beta_2)$ for all $\beta \in (\beta_1, \beta_2)$ if $\beta_1 = -\infty$ and $\beta_2 \in \mathbb{R}$; (iv) $\mathcal{I}(\beta) \subset \mathcal{I}(\beta_1)$ for all $\beta \in (\beta_1, \beta_2)$ if $\beta_2 = \infty$ and $\beta_1 \in \mathbb{R}$.
canonical_claim.definitions_needed: Standing assumptions: $\Delta^2(\beta)$ (15), $\Delta_m^{*2}(\beta)$ (16), Assumption 6, 'distinct' AR functions and their intersections (Remark 7), $\hat\eta^*_{1-\alpha}(\beta, Z)$ (13), $\hat I^*_{1-\alpha}(Z)$ (14), $\mathcal{I}(\beta)$ (17) (main pp. 12-14). $\mathrm{CS}^*$ 'denote[s] the confidence set defined in (5.14)', that is, $\hat I^*_{1-\alpha}(Z)$ of (14) (Supplement p. 45). $M$, the simulated assignments and $\alpha \in (0, 1)$ are fixed. Lemma 1 is target P002-T27. 'No intersection between the AR functions in $(\beta_1, \beta_2)$' means that there are no $\beta \in (\beta_1, \beta_2)$ and indices $m, s \in [M]$ with $\Delta_m^{*2}$ and $\Delta_s^{*2}$ distinct functions and $\Delta_m^{*2}(\beta) = \Delta_s^{*2}(\beta)$ (Remark 7, main p. 14). Under Assumption 6 each $\Delta_m^{*2}$ is a continuous function on $\mathbb{R}$ (main p. 14: 'This assumption implies that $\Delta^2(\beta)$ and each $\Delta_m^{*2}(\beta)$ are continuous functions on $\mathbb{R}$'). $\alpha \in (0, 1)$ and the $M$ simulated assignments are fixed. [Proof as printed, Supplement p. 45 (PDF p. 25), Section H.1] If there is no intersection among the distinct AR functions on the interval $(\beta_1, \beta_2)$, the ranking of the values of the curves at each $\beta$ remains the same, and hence the index set $\mathcal{I}(\beta)$ remains the same. This shows the first claim. The second statement follows by the fact that for all $t \in \mathcal{I}(\beta)$, the collection of squared AR statistics that are less than or equal to $\Delta_t^{*2}(\beta)$ for all $\beta \in (\beta_1, \beta_2)$ will also be less than or equal to $\Delta_t^{*2}(\beta)$ for $\beta = \beta_1$ and $\beta = \beta_2$, by continuity. Similarly, the collection of squared AR statistics that are larger than or equal to $\Delta_t^{*2}(\beta)$ for all $\beta \in (\beta_1, \beta_2)$ will also be weakly dominating on the boundary by continuity. Thus, $t \in \mathcal{I}(\beta_1)$ and $t \in \mathcal{I}(\beta_2)$, by the definition of $\mathcal{I}$ in (5.17) [that is, (17)], where we note that $\hat\eta^*_{1-\alpha}(\beta, Z)$ cannot be strictly smaller than $|\Delta_t^*(\beta)|$ because otherwise there would be a contradiction. The arguments are similar if $\beta_1 = -\infty$ or $\beta_2 = \infty$.
canonical_claim.note: An exact statement about $M$ continuous real functions and the order statistic (13): it does not use the form (16) of the AR functions beyond continuity (and, for the finiteness of intersections used elsewhere, their being ratios of quadratics with positive denominators). Both readers followed the proof and it held up. A convenient equivalent description of the index set for a formalization: $m \in \mathcal{I}(\beta)$ if and only if $\#\{s : |\Delta_s^*(\beta)| \le |\Delta_m^*(\beta)|\} \ge (1 - \alpha)M$ and $\#\{s : |\Delta_s^*(\beta)| < |\Delta_m^*(\beta)|\} < (1 - \alpha)M$; state it as a lemma if used. canonical_claim.statement: [As printed, main p. 17] Theorem 3. Without covariates and under Assumption 6 in the Supplementary Material, the confidence set CS returned by Algorithm 1 or 2 is equal to that in (14). With covariates and under Assumption 7 in the Supplementary Material, the confidence set CS returned by Algorithm 3 or 4 in the Supplementary Material is equal to that in equation (F.4) of the Supplementary Material. [Algorithm 1 as printed, main p. 15] Algorithm 1. Constructing confidence set (14). Require: Observed data $\{Y_i, D_i, Z_i\}_{i\in[n]}$, simulated assignments $\{Z_{im}^*\}_{i\in[n],m\in[M]}$. Step 1: For every $s, t \in [M]$ that define distinct AR functions $\Delta_s^{*2}(\beta)$ and $\Delta_t^{*2}(\beta)$, calculate their intersections. If there is no intersection among any pair of AR functions, choose any $\beta \in \mathbb{R}$ and $m \in \mathcal{I}(\beta)$, return $\mathrm{CS} = \{\beta : |\Delta^2(\beta)| \le |\Delta_m^{*2}(\beta)|\}$ and break. Step 2: Label the intersections $\{\beta_i\}_{i=1}^K$ in increasing order. Denote the intervals that result by $\{[\beta_i, \beta_{i+1}]\}_{i=0}^K$ with $\beta_0 = -\infty$ and $\beta_{K+1} = \infty$. Step 3: For each interval $[\beta_i, \beta_{i+1}]$: If $\beta_i \ne -\infty$ and $\beta_{i+1} \ne +\infty$: Calculate $\mathcal{I}((\beta_i + \beta_{i+1})/2)$, defined in (17). Select any $m_i$ such that $m_i \in \mathcal{I}((\beta_i + \beta_{i+1})/2)$. If $\beta_i = \beta_0 = -\infty$: Select any $m_i \in \mathcal{I}(\beta_1 - 1)$. If $\beta_{i+1} = \beta_{K+1} = +\infty$: Select any $m_i \in \mathcal{I}(\beta_K + 1)$. Step 4: For each interval $\{[\beta_i, \beta_{i+1}]\}_{i=0}^K$: Find $\mathrm{CS}_i = \{\beta : |\Delta^2(\beta)| \le |\Delta_{m_i}^{*2}(\beta)|, \beta \in [\beta_i, \beta_{i+1}]\}$. Step 5: Return $\mathrm{CS} = \bigcup_{i=0}^K \mathrm{CS}_i$. [Algorithm 2 as printed, main p. 16] Algorithm 2. Constructing confidence set (14). Require: Observed data $\{Y_i, D_i, Z_i\}_{i\in[n]}$, simulated assignments $\{Z_{im}^*\}_{i\in[n],m\in[M]}$. Step 1: For every $s, t \in [M]$ that define distinct AR functions. Calculate the intersections and collect them into a set $\mathcal{J}$. If $\mathcal{J}$ is empty, choose any $\beta \in \mathbb{R}$ and $m \in \mathcal{I}(\beta)$, return $\mathrm{CS} = \{\beta : |\Delta^2(\beta)| \le |\Delta_m^{*2}(\beta)|\}$ and break. Step 2: Label the intersections $\{\beta_i\}_{i=1}^K$ in increasing order. Denote the intervals that result by $\{[\beta_i, \beta_{i+1}]\}_{i=0}^K$ with $\beta_0 = -\infty$ and $\beta_{K+1} = \infty$. Step 3: Set $e_0 = -\infty$ and let $m_1$ be any element in $\mathcal{I}(\beta_1 - 1)$. Step 4: For $i = 1, \ldots, \infty$: Find the set of intersections: $\mathcal{C}_i = \left\{\beta \in \mathbb{R} : \exists m \in [M] \setminus \{m_i\},\ \beta > e_{i-1}\ \text{such that}\ \Delta_m^{*2}(\beta) = \Delta_{m_i}^{*2}(\beta)\ \text{and}\ \Delta_m^{*2}, \Delta_{m_i}^{*2}\ \text{are distinct}\right\}$. If $\mathcal{C}_i$ is empty: Record $([e_{i-1}, \infty), m_i)$ and exit the loop. Else: Set $e_i = \min(\mathcal{C}_i)$ and record $\{[e_{i-1}, e_i], m_i\}$. Set $\mathcal{E}_i = \{j \in \mathcal{J}, j > e_i\}$. If $\mathcal{E}_i$ is empty: Set $m_{i+1}$ to be any element of $\mathcal{I}(e_i + 1)$. Else: Set $V_i = \min(\mathcal{E}_i)$. Set $m_{i+1}$ to be any element in $\mathcal{I}((e_i + V_i)/2)$. Step 5: For each interval-index pair in $([e_k, e_{k+1}], m_k)$ recorded in the previous steps: Find $\mathrm{CS}_k = \{\beta : |\Delta^2(\beta)| \le |\Delta_{m_k}^{*2}(\beta)|, \beta \in [e_k, e_{k+1}]\}$. Step 6: Return $\mathrm{CS} = \bigcup_{i=1}^{n_I}\mathrm{CS}_i$, where $n_I$ is the number of for-loop iterations.

Lemma 1 is target P002-T27. Assumption 6 is stated in the main text (Section 5.2, main p. 14), not in the Supplementary Material; Assumption 7 is in the Supplement (p. 43). In Step 1 of both algorithms the comparison is of squared statistics: $|\Delta^2(\beta)| \le |\Delta_m^{*2}(\beta)|$ is equivalent to $|\Delta(\beta)| \le |\Delta_m^*(\beta)|$. [main p. 15] There are at most $M$ draws of assignments, so we have at most $4M^2$ possible intersections. We can sort the $K$ intersections on the real line and divide the real line into $K + 1$ intervals $\{[\beta_i, \beta_{i+1}]\}_{i=0}^K$, where $\beta_0 \equiv -\infty$ and $\beta_{K+1} \equiv \infty$. canonical_claim.statement: [As printed, main p. 8] Theorem 1. Fix $\alpha \in (0, 1)$, $\delta < 1$, $r \in (0, 1/2]$ and $A > 0$. Let $\Theta_n(\delta, r, A)$ be the parameter space of models that satisfy Assumptions 1-4 with these constants. Then $\lim_{n\to\infty}\inf_{\beta\in\mathbb{R}}\inf_{\{\theta\in\Theta_n(\delta,r,A):\,\bar\beta(\theta)=\beta\}}\mathbb{P}_\theta\{\beta \in I^*_{1-\alpha}(Z)\} = 1 - \alpha$. Remark 3. The infimum of the coverage rates of the confidence sets is equal to $1 - \alpha$ because some constant-additive-effect models belong to the set $\Theta_n(\delta, r, A)$. In the design-based setting, the variance is not identified, and a conservative variance bound must instead be estimated (Aronow et al., 2014; Imbens & Rubin, 2015). The asymptotic coverage rate is bounded below by $1 - \alpha$ for many data-generating processes, and is exactly $1 - \alpha$ when the data are generated under a constant-additive-effect model.
